passage:
For most of the twentieth century, the dominant view among neurobiologists held that the adult mammalian brain was essentially fixed in its architecture — that once the critical period of early development had closed, neurons neither regenerated nor formed substantially new connections. This doctrine of neural immutability shaped clinical practice for decades, undergirding the widespread assumption that damage from stroke or traumatic injury was, at the cellular level, permanent.

Subsequent research has dramatically complicated this picture. In the 1990s, investigators working with rodent models demonstrated that the hippocampus (a brain region associated with memory formation and spatial navigation) continued to generate new neurons well into adulthood, a phenomenon termed adult neurogenesis. Initially greeted with skepticism, the finding was replicated across multiple species and eventually confirmed in humans through an indirect but ingenious method: researchers measured the incorporation of carbon-14 into hippocampal neurons, exploiting the spike in atmospheric carbon-14 produced by above-ground nuclear testing in the mid-twentieth century as a kind of natural timestamp. Neurons that incorporated elevated carbon-14 had therefore been born after those tests began, establishing that hippocampal neurogenesis persisted into at least middle adulthood.

However, the functional significance of these new neurons remains contested. One hypothesis holds that adult-born neurons contribute to pattern separation — the brain's ability to encode similar experiences as distinct memories rather than conflating them. According to this hypothesis, the heightened plasticity of immature neurons allows them to form new memory traces without interfering with existing ones. A competing account emphasizes that newborn neurons participate in forgetting as much as in remembering: by integrating into established hippocampal circuits, they may destabilize older memories, thereby clearing the way for new learning. Experiments with mice in which neurogenesis was artificially suppressed showed impairment in both the acquisition of new spatial memories and the timely extinction of conditioned fear responses, a result consistent with the second hypothesis but not conclusive on its own.

A key limitation of current research is that the rate of adult neurogenesis appears to vary considerably across individuals and declines sharply with age, chronic stress, and certain disease states. Whether interventions that promote neurogenesis — among them aerobic exercise, environmental enrichment, and some classes of antidepressant medication — actually improve memory or emotional resilience in humans remains an open question. The biology is suggestive, but the translation from rodent model to clinical application has proven more difficult than early optimism implied.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately states the main point of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Adult neurogenesis in the hippocampus was confirmed by measuring the incorporation of atmospheric carbon-14 into newly formed neurons.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Although the adult mammalian brain was long thought to be structurally fixed, evidence for ongoing neurogenesis has emerged, though the functional role of new neurons is still debated.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The doctrine of neural immutability led clinicians to underestimate the capacity of the brain to recover from stroke and traumatic injury.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Aerobic exercise and environmental enrichment promote adult neurogenesis and may improve memory and emotional resilience in humans.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Two competing hypotheses attempt to explain the function of adult-born neurons, and current experimental evidence decisively supports one over the other.

explanations.correct: The passage moves from the old doctrine of neural immutability (paragraph 1), to the discovery of adult neurogenesis and its confirmation (paragraphs 2–3), to the unresolved debate over its function and the limits of current research (paragraphs 3–4). Choice B captures both the overturning of the old view and the ongoing uncertainty about functional significance.
explanations.A: Too narrow — the carbon-14 method is one piece of evidence in paragraph 2, not the main point of the whole passage.
explanations.C: Too narrow — this is background context from paragraph 1, not the central argument of the passage.
explanations.D: Too narrow and too strong — these interventions are mentioned only speculatively in the final paragraph; the passage does not endorse them as proven benefits.
explanations.E: Distorts the passage — the passage explicitly says the mouse experiments are 'not conclusive on their own,' so no hypothesis is decisively supported.

questions.questionStem: According to the passage, the carbon-14 method used to confirm adult neurogenesis in humans relied on which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: the injection of radioactive tracers into hippocampal tissue taken from living patients

choices.label: B
choices.text: the detection of elevated carbon-14 in neurons formed after atmospheric nuclear testing began

choices.label: C
choices.text: a comparison of carbon-14 levels in hippocampal neurons of young adults versus elderly patients

choices.label: D
choices.text: the measurement of carbon-14 decay rates in neurons to determine the total lifespan of individual cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: the replication of rodent neurogenesis findings in human tissue using radioactive isotope labeling

explanations.correct: The passage states that researchers 'measured the incorporation of carbon-14 into hippocampal neurons, exploiting the spike in atmospheric carbon-14 produced by above-ground nuclear testing' as a natural timestamp. Neurons containing elevated carbon-14 were therefore born after that testing period began.
explanations.A: The passage describes an indirect method using naturally occurring environmental carbon-14, not injected tracers.
explanations.C: The passage does not describe a comparison between age groups; it uses carbon-14 levels as a birth-date marker.
explanations.D: The method timestamps when neurons were born, not how long individual cells live — a plausible-sounding but inaccurate description.
explanations.E: The method was applied to human tissue, but the passage does not describe it as a replication of a rodent procedure; it is described as an independent confirmatory approach.

questions.questionStem: The passage most strongly suggests that, prior to the 1990s research on hippocampal neurogenesis, neurobiologists would have been most likely to believe which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Neurons in the hippocampus are more susceptible to damage than neurons in other brain regions.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Memory formation depends on the formation of new neurons rather than the strengthening of existing synaptic connections.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Any neurons lost to injury or disease in an adult brain would not be replaced by newly generated cells.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Pattern separation in the hippocampus is primarily accomplished by the immature neurons generated during early development.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The hippocampus undergoes less structural change during early development than do other brain regions.

explanations.correct: The passage states that the doctrine of neural immutability held that 'neurons neither regenerated nor formed substantially new connections' after early development, and that this view supported the assumption that brain damage was 'at the cellular level, permanent.' The natural implication is that lost neurons would not be replaced.
explanations.A: The passage never distinguishes hippocampal vulnerability from that of other regions; this is outside the scope of what is stated.
explanations.B: This inverts the old doctrine — neurobiologists held that neurons did not regenerate, which would make synaptic strengthening the only mechanism, not new neuron generation.
explanations.D: Pattern separation is introduced as a hypothesis about adult-born neurons and is not discussed in the context of the pre-1990s view.
explanations.E: The passage says nothing about comparative developmental rates across brain regions.

questions.questionStem: The passage states that experiments in which neurogenesis was artificially suppressed in mice produced which one of the following results?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Mice became unable to form any new long-term memories but retained existing spatial memories.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Mice showed impairment in acquiring new spatial memories and in extinguishing conditioned fear responses.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Mice experienced accelerated loss of older memories, consistent with the pattern-separation hypothesis.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Mice showed no measurable change in memory performance, calling both competing hypotheses into doubt.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Mice demonstrated enhanced retention of established memories alongside reduced capacity for new learning.

explanations.correct: The passage states explicitly: 'Experiments with mice in which neurogenesis was artificially suppressed showed impairment in both the acquisition of new spatial memories and the timely extinction of conditioned fear responses.'
explanations.A: The passage mentions impairment in acquiring new spatial memories but does not say existing memories were retained intact; the framing of 'unable to form any' overstates the finding.
explanations.C: Loss of older memories is associated with the 'forgetting' hypothesis, not with pattern separation; more importantly, the passage does not state this occurred in the suppression experiments.
explanations.D: Contradicts the passage, which reports clear impairments.
explanations.E: The passage does not describe enhanced retention of established memories as a result of neurogenesis suppression.

questions.questionStem: The author's attitude toward the prospect of translating neurogenesis research into clinical treatments for humans can best be described as

choices.label: A
choices.text: enthusiastic endorsement, given the breadth of interventions already shown to promote neurogenesis

choices.label: B
choices.text: measured skepticism, acknowledging suggestive biological evidence while noting that clinical application has proved difficult

choices.label: C
choices.text: dismissive pessimism, arguing that the rodent model is fundamentally unsuitable for drawing conclusions about humans

choices.label: D
choices.text: cautious optimism, predicting that advances in antidepressant pharmacology will soon resolve the outstanding uncertainty

choices.label: E
choices.text: impartial neutrality, presenting the evidence for and against clinical translation without any evaluative stance

explanations.correct: The final paragraph uses the phrase 'the biology is suggestive' (acknowledging the evidence) alongside 'translation from rodent model to clinical application has proven more difficult than early optimism implied' (noting the difficulty). This combination of acknowledgment and caution fits 'measured skepticism.'
explanations.A: Overstates the author's tone — no interventions are described as proven, and the author explicitly flags an 'open question.'
explanations.C: Too negative — the author does not call the rodent model 'fundamentally unsuitable'; they say translation has proven difficult, a softer claim.
explanations.D: The passage does not predict resolution from antidepressant pharmacology; antidepressants are mentioned only as one possible intervention under study.
explanations.E: The author is not neutral — the phrase 'more difficult than early optimism implied' conveys a mild critical evaluation of overconfident prior claims.

questions.questionStem: The author's mention of pattern separation in paragraph three serves primarily to

choices.label: A
choices.text: illustrate that the hippocampus performs multiple cognitive functions beyond memory storage

choices.label: B
choices.text: introduce the first of two competing hypotheses about the functional role of adult-born neurons

choices.label: C
choices.text: provide evidence that adult neurogenesis has been definitively confirmed in human subjects

choices.label: D
choices.text: explain why the carbon-14 method was considered an indirect way to study neurogenesis

choices.label: E
choices.text: suggest that the immature neurons produced in adulthood are structurally identical to those produced in early development

explanations.correct: Pattern separation is introduced immediately after the transition 'One hypothesis holds that adult-born neurons contribute to pattern separation.' Its function is to name and describe the first of the two competing accounts of what new neurons do — setting up the contrast with the 'forgetting' hypothesis that follows.
explanations.A: While the passage implies multiple hippocampal functions, this is not why pattern separation is introduced here; the discussion is specifically about the role of new neurons, not hippocampal functions generally.
explanations.C: Pattern separation is a functional hypothesis, not evidence for the existence of neurogenesis; confirmation is handled in paragraph 2.
explanations.D: The carbon-14 method is discussed in paragraph 2 and is unrelated to the pattern-separation mention.
explanations.E: The passage contrasts the 'heightened plasticity of immature neurons' with established neurons, but does not claim structural identity with developmentally produced neurons.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, would most strengthen the hypothesis that adult-born hippocampal neurons contribute primarily to pattern separation rather than to forgetting?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Individuals with higher rates of hippocampal neurogenesis exhibit more rapid extinction of fear-conditioned responses than those with lower rates.

choices.label: B
choices.text: In studies where neurogenesis is enhanced, subjects show improved ability to distinguish between highly similar memories while older memories remain intact.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The rate of adult neurogenesis declines significantly under conditions of chronic stress, which is also associated with memory impairment.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Suppression of neurogenesis in mice leads to a prolonged retention of conditioned fear responses beyond what is typically observed.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Adult-born neurons integrate into hippocampal circuits within weeks of their formation, at which point their electrical properties resemble those of mature neurons.

explanations.correct: The pattern-separation hypothesis predicts that new neurons help encode similar experiences as distinct memories. If enhanced neurogenesis improves the ability to distinguish between similar memories while leaving older memories undisturbed, this directly supports the pattern-separation account and undermines the competing forgetting account (which would predict destabilization of older memories).
explanations.A: Faster fear extinction supports the 'forgetting' hypothesis — that new neurons help clear old memories — not the pattern-separation hypothesis.
explanations.C: This establishes a correlation between neurogenesis rate and memory impairment under stress, but does not distinguish between the two hypotheses; both would predict memory problems when neurogenesis declines.
explanations.D: Prolonged retention of fear responses following neurogenesis suppression is consistent with the forgetting hypothesis (new neurons normally aid in clearing old conditioned responses), not the pattern-separation hypothesis.
explanations.E: This describes the timeline of neuron maturation but does not bear on whether new neurons are specifically used for pattern separation versus forgetting.
